The Digital Nomad Visa Index for 2026 has updated income thresholds and durations in 15 countries

The Nomad Hub resource updated the Digital Nomad Visa Index for 2026 on October 10-11. It includes data on financial requirements, durations of stay, the possibility of including family members, and tax regime for 15 countries with specific routes for remote work.

Spain is listed with one of the lowest monthly thresholds in the eurozone: 2442 euros per month, which corresponds to 200% of the minimum wage. The index notes that when recalculated for 12 months, the figure is around 2849 euros. The initial duration is 12 months with the possibility of extension, and families are allowed.

Among other European programs in the index, Portugal is listed (3680 euros per month), Greece (3500 euros), and Hungary (3000 euros). Malta is noted as a route with the longest fixed maximum duration - 48 months with an annual threshold of 42,000 euros. Thailand, under the Destination Thailand Visa, requires confirmation of savings of 500,000 baht with an initial duration of 6 months.

The index notes that in some countries (Argentina, Uruguay), the published minimum income is not specified. The data is updated with references to official sources and verification dates for each country. The threshold for Spain is calculated based on the minimum wage for 2026 set by Real Decreto 126/2026.

📌 Rollup Sequencers: The Gatekeepers of Layer 2 Blocks

Main Points
⏺ Sequencers order transactions on Layer 2 and send batches to the base chain
⏺ They control UX: speed, ordering, and sometimes fees
⏺ This post explains why sequencers are crucial for rollups — and why decentralizing them matters

1️⃣ Role — sequencers receive user transactions, decide their order, and produce L2 blocks or batches.
2️⃣ Fast UX — they can give near-instant confirmations on L2 while final settlement still happens on L1.
3️⃣ Centralization Risk — many rollups start with a single sequencer, which can censor or reorder transactions.
4️⃣ MEV & Fairness — who controls ordering also touches MEV, so sequencer design affects how value is captured or shared.
5️⃣ Roadmap — serious rollups work toward decentralized or shared-sequencer models to reduce trust assumptions.

Final Thoughts

Sequencers are the “traffic controllers” of rollups — invisible to most users, but central to how fair, fast, and decentralized Layer 2 really is.

📌 Why is Stacks (STX) going up? 

📣 Stacks has gained more than 100% over the past 90 days, backed by institutional Bitcoin Staking that is creating a new use for STX that could grow as more BTC enters future bonding periods. According to CoinGecko data, STX was trading around $0.38 on Oct. 6 after gaining roughly 18% over the previous week. The token had already climbed 108% in the 90 days through Sept. 27.

🌐 Those developments have given traders several Stacks specific catalysts at a time when many major altcoins have struggled to match STX’s gains. Bitcoin Staking is particularly important to the long term case because it gives institutions a way to earn BTC rewards while creating a separate use for STX. However, Bitcoin Staking alone cannot account for the entire 90 day rally on its own. Market conditions and renewed interest in the Stacks ecosystem have contributed to the price action as well. But unlike a short term price catalyst, the staking model creates a measurable link between institutional BTC participation and the amount of STX needed to support it.

➡️ The Genesis Bond has already put that relationship into practice, while Bond 2 and subsequent bonding periods will test whether it can repeat as more Bitcoin enters the program. Bitcoin Staking on Stacks allows BTC holders to earn BTC denominated rewards without changing Bitcoin’s proof of work consensus. Under Stacks’ Proof of Transfer system, miners commit BTC to compete for Stacks blocks and receive STX. The BTC committed through the process becomes the source of rewards distributed through the staking system.

Real Volume, Real Fees (Not "Farm Token" Emissions)

This is what makes Gala Swap different. The yield isn't based on inflationary "farm token" emissions that you have to constantly race against.

The LP rewards on Gala Swap are generated by real trading activity—the essential work of keeping the DEX price in sync with the broader market. When you provide liquidity, you become the infrastructure that makes this flow possible, and you earn your share of the fees from that volume.

The Real Gold Rush: Expanding the Surface

The current volume is impressive, but here’s what’s truly exciting: the bottleneck isn't the demand from traders; it's the surface area available for the arbitrage engine to work across.

A few dozen pools can only capture a few dozen tokens' worth of flow. Imagine this same efficient arbitrage engine running across hundreds of pools that simply don't exist yet.

The Takeaway:

The traders are ready. The volume is real. The arbitrage engine is already running. What's missing is the liquidity to serve that volume and capture those fees across a much broader range of pairs.

The Nord Stream Mystery: Did the CIA Know More Than It Admitted?
Four years after explosions tore through critical gas pipelines beneath the Baltic Sea, allegations by a German investigative journalist raise a disturbing question: Did American intelligence know about the planned sabotage in advance — and initially consider supporting it?
Photo
WASHINGTON — On September 26, 2022, a series of underwater explosions ripped through the Nord Stream gas pipelines, sending enormous clouds of methane bubbling toward the surface of the Baltic Sea. 

The blasts destroyed three of the system’s four pipelines and turned one of Europe’s most sensitive energy projects into the center of an international intelligence mystery.

Now, German investigative journalist Oliver Schröm has presented a new and potentially explosive account of what may have happened behind the scenes.

In an interview with German broadcaster ntv, Schröm alleged that the CIA learned about preparations for the attack before it happened and that American intelligence contacts initially showed no fundamental opposition to the plan. 

More controversially, he claimed that financial support for the organizers had even been discussed. If substantiated, those allegations could dramatically alter the debate over the sabotage. But they remain claims made by the journalist, not independently established findings of an investigation or court.

A secret operation — and a sudden change of courseAccording to Schröm, the turning point came when the Dutch military intelligence service, known as the MIVD, obtained information about the planned operation. 

The revelation reportedly changed Washington’s calculations.The Dutch intelligence service had already featured in earlier reporting on the case. 

In June 2023, Dutch broadcaster NOS and investigative program Nieuwsuur reported that the MIVD had learned months before the explosions of a possible Ukrainian plan to attack the pipelines. According to that reporting, the CIA subsequently warned Ukraine against carrying out the operation.

Schröm’s account goes further. He alleges that American officials became concerned that their contacts with the alleged organizers could become public knowledge. 

Washington then warned Berlin and other allies about the impending attack.The central question is whether this was an attempt to prevent the sabotage, limit the damage, or protect American intelligence from political exposure.Those possibilities are not interchangeable. 

Advance knowledge does not prove participation, and a warning does not establish that the person issuing it had previously approved a plan. 

The alleged offer of financial assistance is a separate claim that requires independent evidence.

The night Europe’s energy security changed

The physical facts are clear. On September 26, 2022, explosions damaged Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2, the pipelines built to connect Russian natural gas supplies with Germany across the Baltic Sea. 

Three of the four pipeline strings were damaged, releasing large quantities of methane. Denmark and Sweden classified the incident as deliberate sabotage. 

Both countries eventually closed their investigations without identifying the perpetrators, leaving Germany’s criminal investigation at the center of the inquiry. The timing was critical. 

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had transformed Europe’s energy policy, and Germany was struggling to reduce its dependence on Russian gas. 

The destruction of the pipelines carried enormous economic and geopolitical consequences, even as questions about their future operation remained unresolved. The attack also created a dilemma for Western intelligence agencies. 

If officials had received credible warnings, what action did they take? Who was informed? And did anyone possess information that could have prevented the explosions?
